vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: ast30days-aisa-zh
Version: 1.0.0

The skill bundle contains highly intrusive capabilities, including logic to extract encrypted browser cookies from Chrome, Firefox, and Safari on macOS and Linux (found in scripts/lib/cookie_extract.py, scripts/lib/chrome_cookies.py, and scripts/lib/safari_cookies.py). Additionally, scripts such as scripts/sync.sh and scripts/test-v1-vs-v2.sh perform broad filesystem operations, modifying or backing up files in sensitive application directories like ~/.claude, ~/.openclaw, and ~/.agents. While these features are presented as legacy authentication fallbacks or development utilities, the combination of credential-probing logic and wide-ranging filesystem access exceeds the typical requirements of a research tool. Data is primarily routed through api.aisa.one and api.scrapecreators.com.

llm.summary: The skill largely matches a multi-source social-research purpose, but embedded browser cookie/keychain extraction and legacy auth paths contradict the SKILL.md guidance and create unexplained access to local secrets.

dimensions.detail: Most code modules (Reddit, YouTube, TikTok, GitHub, Polymarket, grounding via AIsa) align with the stated multi-source research purpose. However, the repository contains explicit browser cookie extraction (Chrome/Safari/Firefox) and legacy X/Bird compatibility code that enable reading local browser DBs and macOS Keychain access — capabilities that go beyond the SKILL.md's declared 'required' config (AISA_API_KEY) and its explicit guidance to not recommend cookie scanning.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The runtime SKILL.md instructs running Python scripts and declares AISA_API_KEY as the only required env var, and explicitly says not to recommend browser cookie scanning or device authentication. Despite that, the codebase contains modules that (a) copy and decrypt local browser cookie databases, (b) invoke the macOS 'security' CLI (which can trigger Keychain prompts) and 'openssl', and (c) look for X/Twitter session cookies and other credentials on disk or in process env. Those actions are not advertised in the runtime instructions and could access sensitive local data if the code paths are executed.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no external install spec or network download; this is an instruction-only skill with vendored Python sources included. That avoids arbitrary remote code fetch at install time, but the included code will be present on disk when the skill is installed / enabled.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md declares only AISA_API_KEY as required and lists GH_TOKEN/BSKY/TruthSocial as optional. The code, however, can access other credentials or session tokens via environment variables (AUTH_TOKEN, CT0) or by extracting browser cookies and Keychain data. Those sensitive local access mechanisms are not declared or discussed as required/optional in a consistent way, which is disproportionate to the minimal env requirements advertised.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request always:true and does not declare actions that modify other skills or system-wide agent settings. The cookie-access code is read-only (copies DBs to temp files), and there is no installer that persists new privileged services, but it can still read sensitive local stores at runtime.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill appears to implement a legitimate multi-source research tool, but it includes code to extract browser cookies and access the macOS Keychain (via the 'security' CLI and openssl) and legacy X/Twitter compatibility paths. Those capabilities can expose session cookies and other local secrets even though the SKILL.md states only AISA_API_KEY is required and explicitly advises against cookie scanning. Before installing: (1) Ask the publisher why cookie/keychain extraction and legacy auth paths are included and confirm they are not used by default. (2) Inspect scripts/last30days.py and setup_wizard.py to see whether cookie extraction or local credential probing is triggered automatically. (3) Avoid supplying extra credentials (GH_TOKEN, BSKY app password) unless needed; prefer running searches via the advertised AIsa API. (4) If you must run it, use an isolated environment (container or throwaway VM) and monitor for macOS keychain prompts; remove or disable cookie-extraction modules if you do not want local cookie access. If you need a higher-assurance recommendation, provide the full last30days.py entrypoint so I can check which code paths run by default.
